title: The World's Biggest Car Maker Sells Cars for $1
description:
The world's biggest car maker isn't Toyota. It's a toy company.

Mattel sells more than 16 Hot Wheels every second. That works out to about half a billion cars a year. Every real car factory on Earth combined built about 96 million vehicles in 2025.

The first 16 models launched in 1968 for under a dollar. The basic car still costs about a dollar today.

Sources: Mattel, OICA, Toyota, NPR.
For education only. Not investment advice.

title: The 57 on the Ketchup Bottle Is Made Up
description:
The most famous number in food is made up.

In 1896, Henry Heinz saw a shoe ad on a New York train: 21 styles. He wanted a number too. His company already sold more than 60 products. He picked 57 anyway. Five was his lucky number. Seven was his wife's.

It is still on the bottle today.

Sources: Heinz company history.
For education only. Not investment advice.

title: WD-40 Is Named After 39 Failures
description:
The name on the can is a failure count.

In 1953, a three-person lab in San Diego was trying to stop missiles from rusting. It took 40 attempts. The 40th worked: Water Displacement, 40th formula. WD-40.

They never patented it, so the formula has stayed a trade secret. In 1969 the company renamed itself after its one product.

Sources: WD-40 Company history, Field & Stream, Motor1.

title: A Spring Fell Off a Shelf and Sold 400 in 90 Minutes
description:
A spring fell off a shelf and sold 400 in 90 minutes.

In 1943, engineer Richard James was testing springs to steady instruments on warships. One fell off a shelf and kept walking. His wife Betty named it Slinky. Stores were not interested.

So in 1945 he demonstrated it at Gimbels in Philadelphia. 400 Slinkys at $1 each were gone in 90 minutes.

Sources: Lemelson-MIT, TIME, PBS.
For education only.

title: Bubble Wrap Was Invented as Wallpaper
description:
This was supposed to go on your walls.

In 1957, two engineers in New Jersey sealed two shower curtains together and trapped air bubbles inside. Their plan was textured wallpaper. Nobody bought it. Plan two was greenhouse insulation. That failed too.

Then IBM had to ship a delicate new computer, and Bubble Wrap finally got a job.

Sources: Smithsonian Magazine, Mental Floss.
For education only. Not investment advice.

title: Wrigley Never Meant to Sell Gum
description:
The world's biggest gum company never meant to sell gum.

In 1891, William Wrigley Jr. sold soap in Chicago and threw in free baking powder. People wanted the baking powder more. So he sold baking powder and threw in free chewing gum. People wanted the gum more.

So he dropped everything and sold only gum. By 1908, one flavor topped $1 million a year.

Source: Britannica.
For education only. Not investment advice.

title: This Pen Has Sold 100 Billion Times
description:
This pen has sold more than 100 billion times.

The Bic Cristal launched in France in 1950. Six sides, like a pencil. A tiny hole in the barrel keeps the ink flowing. The hole in the cap is there for safety: if someone inhales the cap, air can still pass through. Today that is an international standard.

It passed 100 billion in 2006.

Sources: Design Museum, MoMA, Snopes.
For education only. Not investment advice.

title: Listerine Used to Be a Floor Cleaner
description:
Your mouthwash used to clean floors.

Listerine was invented in St. Louis in 1879 as a surgical antiseptic. Later it was sold as a floor cleaner, even a dandruff cure. Sales stayed small.

Then the 1920s ads found a scary word: halitosis. In seven years, revenue went from $115,000 to more than $8 million.

Sources: company history as reported by History Facts and the Federation of Historical Bottle Collectors.

title: PEZ Was Made to Stop Adults Smoking
description:
This candy was made to stop adults smoking.

In 1927, Eduard Haas in Vienna pressed peppermint into tiny bricks and called them PEZ, short for Pfefferminz. The slogan: smoking prohibited, PEZing allowed. In 1949 the dispenser arrived, shaped like a lighter.

America was not interested, so they added fruit flavors and cartoon heads for kids.

Sources: PEZ company history, Lemelson-MIT.

title: This Mint Is Almost All Sugar. The Label Says 0g.
description:
This mint is almost all sugar, and the label says zero.

In the US, a serving is one single mint. One Tic Tac weighs about 0.49 grams. Under the labelling rule, less than half a gram of sugar per serving can be printed as zero.

It is completely legal. And sugar is still first on the ingredient list.

US label only. Sources: FDA nutrition labelling rule (21 CFR 101.9), Tasting Table.
For education only. Not health advice.
